How the estimates work

Source: vignettes/articles/estimation.Rmd
estimation.Rmd
library(drawn)

This article sets out what ht_total() and ht_mean() compute, which variance estimator each design gets and why, and how each one was checked. Everything here is design-based: the population values are fixed, and the only randomness is which rows the design selected (Särndal, Swensson and Wretman 1992).

The estimators

A design gives every frame row \(k\) an inclusion probability \(\pi_k\) — the chance it lands in the sample — and every pair of rows a joint probability \(\pi_{kl}\). inclusion_prob() and joint_prob() compute them from the design and the frame, before anything is drawn.

The total is the Horvitz-Thompson estimator (Horvitz and Thompson 1952):

\[\hat Y = \sum_{k \in s} \frac{y_k}{\pi_k}.\]

It is unbiased for the frame total provided every row has \(\pi_k > 0\). That proviso is why draw() warns when a stratum is allocated no rows, and why sample_summary() counts unreachable rows.

The mean defaults to the Hájek estimator (Hájek 1971), a ratio of two Horvitz-Thompson totals:

\[\hat{\bar Y} = \frac{\sum_{s} y_k / \pi_k}{\sum_{s} 1 / \pi_k}.\]

Its variance is the variance of the Horvitz-Thompson total of the linearised residuals \(z_k = (y_k - \hat{\bar Y}) / \hat N\) (Deville 1999), so every variance estimator below serves means as well as totals. A proportion is the mean of a 0/1 variable.

Domains — sites, regions, months — use the whole sample with \(y\) set to zero outside the domain: \(z_k = y_k \cdot 1[k \in d]\) for a total, and the corresponding residual for a mean (Särndal et al. 1992, section 10.3). Cutting the sample into pieces first would treat the number of rows that fell in each piece as fixed, which it is not.

Which variance estimator, for which design

Design Estimator method Status
simple, stratified, temporal, spatial, reservoir, multistage Sen-Yates-Grundy with exact \(\pi_{kl}\) "analytic" exact, unbiased
cluster between-cluster form over cluster totals "analytic" exact, unbiased
cluster with balanced = TRUE, multistage with a take that depends on the clusters selected two-stage formula at each cluster’s take, weights conditional on the clusters selected "analytic" unbiased
weighted, "poisson" \(\sum (1-\pi_k) y_k^2 / \pi_k^2\) "analytic" exact, unbiased
weighted, "systematic" Deville (1999) "deville" approximation
systematic successive differences (Wolter 2007) "successive difference" approximation
systematic, n_starts of 2 or more random groups (Wolter 2007) "analytic" exact, unbiased
stratified, within = design_systematic() successive differences within strata "successive difference" approximation
spread local means (Stevens and Olsen 2003) "local mean" approximation, conservative
certainty whatever rest uses as rest as rest
any, on request or as fallback jackknife, stratified where there are strata "jackknife" approximation

Sen-Yates-Grundy

For a fixed-size design with known joint probabilities,

\[\hat V_{\mathrm{SYG}} = \frac12 \sum_{k \ne l \in s} \frac{\pi_k \pi_l - \pi_{kl}}{\pi_{kl}} \left(\frac{y_k}{\pi_k} - \frac{y_l}{\pi_l}\right)^2\]

is unbiased whenever every \(\pi_{kl} > 0\) (Sen 1953; Yates and Grundy 1953). For stratified simple random sampling it reduces to the textbook \(\sum_h N_h^2 (1 - f_h) s_h^2 / n_h\), with \(s_h^2\) the variance of \(y\) among the rows sampled in stratum \(h\). Simple random, reservoir and spatial samples are the case of a single stratum, and temporal intervals are strata. For design_multistage() with the same take of \(m\) rows from each of \(a\) clusters selected out of \(A\), it reduces to the two-stage formula

\[\hat V = A^2 \left(1 - \frac{a}{A}\right) \frac{s_t^2}{a} + \frac{A}{a} \sum_{i \in s} N_i^2 \left(1 - \frac{m}{N_i}\right) \frac{s_i^2}{m},\]

with \(s_t^2\) the variance of the estimated cluster totals \(N_i \bar y_i\) and \(s_i^2\) the variance within cluster \(i\). drawn computes these forms, which take time and memory in proportion to the number of sampled rows. The sum over pairs needs matrices with a row and a column per sampled row, more than a gigabyte at 4,000 rows.

Under proportional allocation, an \(n\) that does not divide by the number of clusters, a cluster smaller than the take, or design_cluster(balanced = TRUE), the take \(m_i\) from cluster \(i\) depends on which clusters were selected. A row’s inclusion probability then averages over every selection; only the balanced design has a closed form for it, and none of them has one for the joint probabilities. draw(weights = TRUE) weights such a sample conditional on the selection, \(\pi_k = (a/A)\, m_i / N_i\), so the estimated total is \(A/a\) times the sum of the estimated totals of the selected clusters, unbiased given the selection and so over every selection. The formula above, with \(m_i\) in place of \(m\), is unbiased for its variance. Given the selection, the estimated cluster totals also vary by the variance within each cluster, so the first term holds \((A/a)^2 (1 - a/A)\) times the within-cluster variances on average, and with the second term that makes \((A/a)^2\) times them, the variance of the estimate given the selection. What remains of the first term is the variance between clusters.

The condition matters. A stratum with one sampled row has no pair inside it, so it silently contributes nothing: with one row in every stratum the sum is exactly zero. drawn declines in that case rather than report it:

set.seed(1)
pop <- data.frame(g = rep(1:10, each = 20), y = rnorm(200, rep(1:10, each = 20), 3))
one_each <- draw(pop, design_stratified("g", n = 10), seed = 1, weights = TRUE)
ht_total(one_each, "y")
#> Horvitz-Thompson total  (stratified design, n = 10)
#>   estimate 957.7274
#>   se       NA
#> 
#>   No variance is available for this sample. 10 strata `1`, `2`, `3`,
#>   `4`, `5`, ... each have a single sampled row, so the variation within
#>   them cannot be measured and leaving them out would understate the
#>   standard error. Draw at least two rows per stratum (min_per_stratum =
#>   2).

Cluster sampling

Taking whole clusters makes the number of rows random whenever clusters differ in size, which violates the fixed-size assumption behind Sen-Yates-Grundy. The cluster is the sampling unit, so the estimator is applied to cluster totals \(u_c = \sum_{k \in c} y_k / \pi_k\): \(\hat V = (1 - a/A)\, a\, s_u^2\), the simple-random form over \(a\) of \(A\) clusters.

Poisson sampling

Rows are selected independently, so \(\pi_{kl} = \pi_k \pi_l\) and the Horvitz-Thompson variance collapses to \(\sum_s (1 - \pi_k) y_k^2 / \pi_k^2\).

Systematic PPS: Deville’s approximation

design_weighted(method = "systematic") shuffles the frame and walks the cumulative probabilities (Madow 1949; Hartley and Rao 1962). Its joint probabilities have no closed form. Deville’s estimator needs only the first-order ones:

\[\hat V = \frac{1}{1 - \sum_s a_k^2} \sum_{k \in s} c_k \left(\frac{y_k}{\pi_k} - \hat A\right)^2, \quad c_k = 1 - \pi_k,\; a_k = \frac{c_k}{\sum_s c_l},\; \hat A = \sum_s a_k \frac{y_k}{\pi_k}.\]

Each row is weighted by its own \(1 - \pi_k\), so rows taken with certainty drop out, as they should. Matei and Tillé (2005) found it the most reliable of the standard approximations for high-entropy designs. It equals sampling::varest().

Systematic sampling: successive differences

A systematic sample has one random start. At an interval \(k\) of 2 or more, neighbouring rows and many other pairs can never be drawn together, so their joint probability is 0 and no design-unbiased variance estimator exists at all. The successive-difference estimator compares each sampled row with its neighbour in the order the design walked (Wolter 2007):

\[\hat V = (1 - f)\, \frac{n}{2(n-1)} \sum_{j=2}^{n} \left(\frac{y_{(j)}}{\pi} - \frac{y_{(j-1)}}{\pi}\right)^2.\]

When \(k\) does not divide the \(N\) rows the design walks, the sample holds \(\lfloor N/k \rfloor\) or \(\lfloor N/k \rfloor + 1\) rows, and the total moves with that count. Successive differences cannot see it, so \(\bar u^2 (r/k)(1 - r/k)\) is added, with \(\bar u\) the mean of \(y/\pi\) over the sample and \(r\) the remainder of \(N/k\). Without the term a constant \(y\) would get a variance of 0.

Sorting the frame on something related to \(y\) is what makes systematic sampling efficient, and this estimator can see that where the simple-random formula cannot:

set.seed(12)
frame <- data.frame(x = runif(400, 0, 100))
frame$y <- frame$x + rnorm(400, 0, 20)
sorted <- design_systematic(interval = 10, order_by = "x")

# The truth, by enumerating all ten starts
starts <- vapply(1:10, function(st) {
  10 * sum(draw(frame, design_systematic(10, start = st, order_by = "x"))$y)
}, numeric(1))
true_var <- mean((starts - mean(starts))^2)

est <- vapply(1:200, function(i) {
  s <- draw(frame, sorted, seed = i, weights = TRUE)
  c(successive = ht_total(s, "y")$variance,
    as_if_srs  = 400^2 * 0.9 * var(s$y) / nrow(s))
}, numeric(2))
round(rowMeans(est) / true_var, 2)
#> successive  as_if_srs 
#>       1.59       5.48

Both are ratios to the true variance. The successive-difference estimator averaged 1.6 times it on this frame and the simple-random formula 5.5 times. Neither is design-unbiased, and how far the successive-difference figure lands from the truth changes from one frame to the next.

Its limits are shared by every estimator from a single systematic sample. A frame that cycles with a period equal to the interval, or one that divides it, puts every row of one sample at the same phase of the cycle, and the estimate runs far low. A period of twice the interval puts neighbouring sampled rows at opposite phases, and it runs high, 29 times the truth in one simulation. A trend so smooth that the random start is almost the only source of variation makes it run low, with no floor. For a straight line with no noise the ratio is \(6k / (n(k + 1))\), about \(6/n\), for \(n\) rows at interval \(k\).

Several starts: random groups

design_systematic(interval = k, n_starts = m) draws \(m\) different starts from \(1, \dots, mk\) and walks each at a step of \(mk\). Every row keeps its probability of \(1/k\), and two rows \(i\) and \(j\) in different residue classes modulo \(mk\) can now be drawn together, with \(\pi_{ij} = (m-1)/(k(mk-1))\). Each start gives a replicate whose own total \(\hat t_r\) estimates \(t\), the sample’s total is their mean \(\bar t\), and

\[\hat V = \left(1 - \frac1k\right) \frac{1}{m(m-1)} \sum_{r=1}^{m} \left(\hat t_r - \bar t\right)^2\]

is the random group estimator (Wolter 2007), unbiased on \(m - 1\) degrees of freedom. It equals the Horvitz-Thompson variance estimator over the exact \(\pi_{ij}\), so method is "analytic". The price is a step \(m\) times as long, so each replicate follows a sorted frame less closely, and few degrees of freedom: with four starts a 95% interval uses \(t_3\).

design_stratified(within = design_systematic(order_by = "x")) instead walks each stratum from a start of its own, at a step of \(N_h / n_h\) rows. The variance is the sum of the strata’s successive-difference approximations, on the degrees of freedom of a stratified sample.

Spatially balanced samples: local means

design_spread() selects by the local pivotal method (Grafström, Lundström and Schelin 2012), which makes neighbours unlikely to be sampled together. That is exactly the gain, and a simple-random variance would throw it away. The local mean estimator compares each sampled row with the mean over its neighbourhood \(N_k\) — itself and its three nearest sampled neighbours:

\[\hat V = \sum_{k \in s} \frac{|N_k|}{|N_k| - 1} \left(\frac{y_k}{\pi_k} - \frac{1}{|N_k|}\sum_{l \in N_k} \frac{y_l}{\pi_l}\right)^2\]

(Stevens and Olsen 2003; Grafström and Schelin 2014). It errs conservative, more so as the sampling fraction grows. Rows that a size column puts past certainty are in every sample, so the sum leaves them out, as rows and as neighbours.

The jackknife

The delete-one-unit jackknife works from the sample alone. Units are clusters where the design has them and rows otherwise, and where the design has strata they are deleted within their stratum, with only that stratum reweighted — the stratified or JKn jackknife (Wolter 2007, chapter 4). Deleting across strata would count the differences between strata as sampling variance, which is what stratifying removes. Each stratum carries its own finite population correction. Units taken with certainty, whether past certainty on size, in a stratum taken whole or in a census, are in every sample, so they are held fixed instead of deleted and the correction counts only the other units. For a stratified design the result equals the analytic figure exactly:

strat <- draw(pop, design_stratified("g", n = 40), seed = 2, weights = TRUE)
c(analytic  = ht_total(strat, "y", variance = "analytic")$se,
  jackknife = ht_total(strat, "y", variance = "jackknife")$se)
#>  analytic jackknife 
#>  78.99364  78.99364

variance = "auto" uses the design’s own estimator, and the jackknife only when that declines — for instance a multistage sample with one row per cluster, where the within-cluster variation cannot be measured and the delete-a-cluster jackknife gives the standard ultimate-cluster approximation. It is refused for systematic samples, whose primary sampling units are their starts rather than their rows, and Poisson samples, whose exact variance it understates.

Confidence intervals

Intervals use Student’s \(t\) on the design’s degrees of freedom — primary sampling units minus strata — rather than the normal distribution (Korn and Graubard 1999). With hundreds of units the two agree; with a handful of clusters the normal interval is badly short:

set.seed(5)
clus <- data.frame(cl = rep(1:24, each = 10))
clus$y <- rep(rnorm(24, 50, 20), each = 10) + rnorm(240, 0, 5)
truth <- sum(clus$y)

hits <- vapply(1:500, function(i) {
  r <- ht_total(draw(clus, design_cluster("cl", n_clusters = 4), seed = i,
                     weights = TRUE), "y")
  c(t = r$ci[1] <= truth && truth <= r$ci[2],
    normal = abs(r$total - truth) <= qnorm(0.975) * r$se)
}, logical(2))
rowMeans(hits)
#>      t normal 
#>  0.960  0.846

Pass df = Inf for the normal interval.

Units taken with certainty count in neither number. They are in every sample and carry no variance, so counting them would make the interval too narrow. With eight certain units among ten, systematic PPS had 9 degrees of freedom where the variance rests on two units, and the interval covered 79%. A sample with no unit below certainty has a variance of 0 and df = Inf.

How it was checked

Every estimator is checked in the package’s tests against the empirical sampling variance of its own estimator over many repeated draws, and every inclusion and joint probability against the observed frequency. A condensed version, run when this page was built, gives the ratio of the average estimated variance to the true variance of the total (1 is perfect) and the coverage of the nominal 95% interval. For the five designs whose joint probabilities have a closed form, the true variance is computed from them, \(\sum_{k,l} \pi_{kl} \frac{y_k}{\pi_k} \frac{y_l}{\pi_l} - Y^2\) over the frame. Systematic PPS and spread have none, and their ratio is to the variance of the simulated totals:

set.seed(7)
N <- 300
frame <- data.frame(
  site = rep(c("a", "b", "c"), times = c(150, 100, 50)),
  cl   = rep(paste0("c", 1:30), each = 10),
  x    = runif(N), yy = runif(N)
)
frame$size <- rgamma(N, 3, 0.2)
frame$y <- 2 * frame$size + 30 * frame$x + rep(rnorm(30, 0, 8), each = 10) +
  rnorm(N, 0, 6)
truth <- sum(frame$y)

designs <- list(
  simple        = design_simple(n = 40),
  stratified    = design_stratified("site", n = 40),
  cluster       = design_cluster("cl", n_clusters = 6),
  multistage    = design_multistage("cl", n_clusters = 8, n = 32),
  pps_poisson   = design_weighted("size", n = 40, method = "poisson"),
  pps_systematic = design_weighted("size", n = 40, method = "systematic"),
  spread        = design_spread(c("x", "yy"), n = 40, scale = FALSE)
)

exact <- c("simple", "stratified", "cluster", "multistage", "pps_poisson")
exact_variance <- function(d) {
  z <- frame$y / inclusion_prob(frame, d)
  sum(joint_prob(frame, d) * outer(z, z)) - truth^2
}

check <- function(name, R = 1000) {
  d <- designs[[name]]
  out <- vapply(seq_len(R), function(i) {
    r <- ht_total(draw(frame, d, seed = i, weights = TRUE), "y")
    c(r$total, r$variance, r$ci[1] <= truth && truth <= r$ci[2])
  }, numeric(3))
  against <- if (name %in% exact) "exact" else "simulated"
  v <- if (name %in% exact) exact_variance(d) else var(out[1, ])
  data.frame(variance_ratio = round(mean(out[2, ]) / v, 2), against,
             coverage = round(mean(out[3, ]), 2))
}
do.call(rbind, setNames(lapply(names(designs), check), names(designs)))
#>                variance_ratio   against coverage
#> simple                   1.01     exact     0.95
#> stratified               0.99     exact     0.95
#> cluster                  0.99     exact     0.94
#> multistage               1.02     exact     0.96
#> pps_poisson              0.99     exact     0.94
#> pps_systematic           1.00 simulated     0.93
#> spread                   1.18 simulated     0.96

Against the exact variance, the ratio’s Monte Carlo error is that of the average estimate alone, under 1.5% here. A ratio to the variance of simulated totals also carries the error of that variance, about 5% at the 1,000 draws used here and 7% to 9% at 400. At 400 draws the cluster and Poisson samples gave ratios of 0.85 and 0.87 to the simulated variance and 0.98 to the exact one. The coverage carries an error of about 0.7 percentage points.

Agreement with survey

as_svydesign() expresses each design in survey’s own terms (Lumley 2004), and the tests assert that the two packages agree to floating point on totals, standard errors, domain estimates and degrees of freedom for every design survey can represent exactly. Units taken with certainty go to survey as one sampling unit per stratum, taken whole, so that neither package counts them among the degrees of freedom. For systematic PPS, survey uses Brewer’s approximation and drawn uses Deville’s. The degrees of freedom still agree. On frames of a few hundred rows with skewed sizes the standard errors of totals usually agree within 0.5%, and usually within 3% where the probabilities below certainty spread widely. Those of means can differ by several percent when the sampling fraction is large. ?as_svydesign has the full table.

survey::as.svrepdesign() cannot build replicate weights from survey’s own PPS and Poisson designs, and for a systematic sample it builds a jackknife that ignores the order of the walk. replicate_weights() builds them from the sample instead: the jackknife above for most designs, and successive differences along the walk for a systematic sample, with no pair joining the two ends of the walk. For a systematic sample the standard error of a total is then the one ht_total() gives by default:

sys <- draw(frame, design_systematic(interval = 10, order_by = "size"),
            seed = 3, weights = TRUE)
rw <- replicate_weights(sys)
rep_des <- survey::svrepdesign(
  data = sys, repweights = rw, weights = ~.weight,
  type = attr(rw, "type"), scale = attr(rw, "scale"),
  rscales = attr(rw, "rscales"), combined.weights = TRUE
)
c(drawn = ht_total(sys, "y")$se,
  survey = as.numeric(survey::SE(survey::svytotal(~y, rep_des))))
#>    drawn   survey 
#> 837.5215 837.5215

Calibration is left to survey too. frame_totals() gives the population totals survey::calibrate() takes, from the frame stored with the sample and over the rows the design could reach, so the totals need not be built by hand. Here size is known for every row of the frame and related to y, and calibrating a simple random sample to its total narrows the standard error:

srs <- draw(frame, design_simple(n = 40), seed = 3, weights = TRUE)
totals <- frame_totals(srs, ~size)
totals
#> (Intercept)        size 
#>     300.000    4471.591
cal <- survey::calibrate(as_svydesign(srs), ~size, population = totals)
c(horvitz_thompson = ht_total(srs, "y")$se,
  calibrated = as.numeric(survey::SE(survey::svytotal(~y, cal))))
#> horvitz_thompson       calibrated 
#>         935.1447         544.2014

With table = TRUE, frame_totals() gives the counts in each cell of its variables instead, for survey::postStratify() and survey::rake().

Fieldwork and missing values

A weighted sample carries its design, so fieldwork results are joined to the sample rather than the sample to the results. add_fieldwork() adds the columns of a results table keyed by an id, in the sample’s own order, and leaves y missing for a sampled row with no result. A sample sent to the field as a CSV file comes back with its rows and its .row column but not its design, and as_drawn() rebuilds it from the design and the frame. Here the sites differ in spend, and site c answered less often:

set.seed(11)
shops <- data.frame(id = 1:600,
                    site = rep(c("a", "b", "c"), times = c(300, 200, 100)))
shops$spend <- round(c(a = 80, b = 120, c = 200)[shops$site] +
                       rnorm(600, 0, 25))
listing <- shops[, c("id", "site")]
by_site <- design_stratified("site", n = 60)
s <- draw(listing, by_site, seed = 1, weights = TRUE)

path <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
write.csv(s, path, row.names = FALSE)
back <- as_drawn(read.csv(path), by_site, listing)

answered <- back$id[back$site != "c" | back$id %% 2 == 0]
results <- shops[shops$id %in% answered, c("id", "spend")]
back <- add_fieldwork(back, results, by = "id")
table(back$site, answered = !is.na(back$spend))
#>    answered
#>     FALSE TRUE
#>   a     0   30
#>   b     0   20
#>   c     7    3

ht_total() refuses the missing values. A total over the rows that answered counts the others as 0, and so is low by about the share of the weight they hold:

ht_total(back, "spend")
#> Error:
#> ! `y` is missing in 7 of the 60 sampled rows. A total over the rows with `y` present counts the others as 0, so it is low by about their share of the weight, 12% here. ht_mean(na_rm = TRUE) estimates the mean over the rows with `y` present, with `by` for domains, as survey's `na.rm = TRUE` does after as_svydesign(). For a total, adjust the weights for nonresponse within weighting classes and estimate from them with as_svydesign(). See "Missing values and nonresponse" in ?ht_total.

ht_mean(na_rm = TRUE) estimates the mean over the rows with spend present, treating them as a domain of the whole sample. The estimate is the Hajek mean over them, and its variance that of the linearised residuals over every sampled row, 0 for the rows left out. survey::svymean(na.rm = TRUE) gives the same estimate and standard error.

ht_mean(back, "spend", na_rm = TRUE)
#> Hajek mean  (stratified design, n = 53)
#>   missing  7 sampled rows left out, assumed missing completely at random
#>   estimate 97.84906
#>   se       5.020657  (analytic)
#>   95% CI  87.79536 to 107.9027  (t, 57 df)
survey::svymean(~spend, as_svydesign(back), na.rm = TRUE)
#>         mean     SE
#> spend 97.849 5.0207

That mean assumes the values are missing completely at random. Here they are not. Site c spends the most and answered least, so the mean is low against the frame’s 113.7. A weighting-class adjustment assumes only that within each class, here each site, whether a row answered is unrelated to its spend. Each row that answered takes on the weight of the rows of its class that did not, and survey estimates from the adjusted .weight:

answer <- !is.na(back$spend)
boost <- tapply(back$.weight, back$site, sum) /
  tapply(back$.weight * answer, back$site, sum)
adjusted <- back
adjusted$.weight[answer] <- adjusted$.weight[answer] *
  boost[adjusted$site[answer]]
des <- as_svydesign(adjusted)
c(mean = coef(survey::svymean(~spend, des, na.rm = TRUE)),
  total = coef(survey::svytotal(~spend, des, na.rm = TRUE)),
  frame_mean = mean(shops$spend), frame_total = sum(shops$spend))
#>  mean.spend total.spend  frame_mean frame_total 
#>    112.1389  67283.3333    113.6683  68201.0000

survey treats the adjusted weights as fixed, so its standard errors leave out that the adjustment factors were estimated from the sample. ht_total() and ht_mean() keep to .prob and warn that .weight was changed.
